  3. 3 Must see within Downtown, SoMa & Union Square · Southeast Asian

    Lunette

    Nite Yun's Cambodian counter in the Ferry Building (successor to Oakland's Nyum Bai) — kuy teav noodle soup and Cambodian fried chicken; Yun a 2025 James Beard Best Chef: California semifinalist.

  4. 4 Must see within Downtown, SoMa & Union Square

    Cable Cars (Powell-Hyde & Powell-Mason)

    The world's last manually operated cable-car system, running since 1873; the Powell-Hyde and Powell-Mason lines climb Nob and Russian hills from the Powell/Market turnaround down to Fisherman's Wharf.

    Your guide’s note A sheave-rehab project (Feb-Jun 2026) causes occasional segment closures with bus shuttles; at least one line stays running.

    Powell Street cable car turnaround, Powell St & Market St, San Francisco, CA 94102

    Recommended by ,

  5. 5 Must see within Downtown, SoMa & Union Square

    Ferry Building Marketplace

    The 1898 Beaux-Arts ferry terminal with its landmark clock tower, reborn as a food hall of local artisans; the Tuesday/Thursday/Saturday farmers' market on the plaza is one of the country's best.

    1 Ferry Building, San Francisco, CA 94111

    Recommended by ,

  6. 6 Must see within Downtown, SoMa & Union Square

    Transamerica Pyramid & Redwood Park

    SF's tallest and most recognizable tower (1972), reopened in 2024 after a $1B restoration; the adjoining half-acre Transamerica Redwood Park, a public grove of coast redwoods with a sculpture, is the free draw.

    Your guide’s note Tower interior is private offices; Redwood Park is the public space.

    600 Montgomery St, San Francisco, CA 94111

    Recommended by ,

    Look for Free, open to pedestrians and fishing.

How we choose

Every place is recommended by named sources (review-aggregator star ratings never count as the recommender), pinned to its door from a published coordinate, and status-checked. Closed places stay, flagged, so you know they’re gone.

Must see
The places to plan a visit around — graded within each area, not across the city.
Worth the detour
Strong picks, worth going out of your way for.
Deep cut
For the curious: smaller, odder, more local.

Within each area, places are ordered by tier, then by number of named sources — never by popularity. Numbers on the cards match the pins on the map. No ratings, prices or opening hours are shown, because the guide doesn’t hold verified ones.

204 sights and 192 places to eat across San Francisco and the northern Peninsula down to San Mateo, each traceable to the source that named it. The city’s food canon runs from the Mission burrito and Chinatown dim sum to cioppino, Tenderloin Vietnamese and the third-wave coffee it helped invent.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. San Francisco’s signature strength is its food canon: the Mission burrito and taqueria belt, Cantonese dim sum in the oldest Chinatown in America, cioppino and Dungeness crab, Tenderloin Vietnamese, the Bay’s famous Burmese, sourdough and the third-wave coffee it helped invent — each led by Michelin, The Infatuation, KQED and the SF Standard. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it happens to serve.

Web-searched and fact-checked

Every place is traceable to a credible source — Michelin, Eater SF, The Infatuation, SF Chronicle, Mercury News, Atlas Obscura and official sites — recorded in data/sources.json (direct map/page fetches are blocked in the build environment, so sources were confirmed via search). Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open.
